summary: Several ICMPv4 message types became obsolete in practice but were never formally retired. This document deprecates them, which tidies up the IANA registry. It updates RFC 792 and RFC 950, obsoletes RFC 1788, and asks that RFC 1788 be moved to Historic status.

plainLanguage.summary: Some old message types in the internet's toolbox are never used anymore. This officially puts them away so the toolbox list is clean.

questions: which icmpv4 message types are deprecated
is icmp information request still used
what replaced icmp address mask request
subtitle: Fifteen unused ICMPv4 message types are formally retired and RFC 1788 goes to Historic.

tldr.problem: Many ICMPv4 message types had become obsolete in practice but were never formally deprecated, leaving clutter in the IANA registry.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists 15 message types, explains why each is obsolete, asks IANA to mark them deprecated, and asks the RFC Editor to make RFC 1788 Historic.
tldr.outcome: The registry is cleaned up, and the formal deprecation can serve as a basis for filtering these packets.

today: RFC 6918 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013. It updates RFC 792 and RFC 950 and obsoletes RFC 1788, and no later RFC is recorded as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Over the years many ICMPv4 message types were specified. A number of them became obsolete in practice but were never formally deprecated. This document deprecates them, "cleaning up" the corresponding IANA registry.

It also updates RFC 792 and RFC 950, obsoletes RFC 1788, and requests that the RFC Editor change the status of RFC 1788 to Historic.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old message types are never used any more. This RFC says so officially so the list can be tidied.

sections.title: Why Each Type Is Obsolete
sections.content:
The discussion draws on publicly available information and information from the requester of each assignment. The reasons fall into a few groups.

  • Superseded by DHCP: Information Request (Type 15) and Information Reply (Type 16), from RFC 792, and Address Mask Request (Type 17) and Reply (Type 18), from RFC 950, which was meant to obtain the subnet mask. DHCP superseded all four for host configuration.
  • Tied to historic or unused protocols: Traceroute (Type 30) from RFC 1393, never widely deployed, whose RFC was made Historic by RFC 6814. Datagram Conversion Error (Type 31) was for TP/IX (RFC 1475), which is Historic.
  • Never widely deployed or implemented: Mobile Host Redirect (32), IPv6 Where-Are-You (33), IPv6 I-Am-Here (34), Mobile Registration Request (35) and Reply (36), Domain Name Request (37) and Reply (38), and SKIP (39).

For Alternate Host Address (Type 6) the RFC says there is no publicly available information.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old messages were replaced by better tools, some belonged to ideas that died, and some were just never used. One has no known story at all.

sections.title: The IANA Request
sections.content:
The RFC formally deprecates the following types and asks IANA to mark them as such in the "Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) Parameters" registry: Types 6, 15, 16, 17, 18, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38 and 39.

The ICMPv4 Source Quench message (Type 4) is not part of this change because it was already deprecated by RFC 6633.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC hands IANA a list of numbers to cross off. One more was already crossed off earlier.

sections.title: RFC 1788 Becomes Historic
sections.content:
RFC 1788 defined the Domain Name Request and Reply messages. This document requests that the RFC Editor change its status to Historic.

RFC 1385 and RFC 1393 already have Historic status. RFC 792 and RFC 950 are not changed to Historic because other parts of those documents are still current.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC for the unused domain-name messages gets retired, but the two bigger RFCs stay because they still have useful parts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document does not modify the security properties of the message types being deprecated. It does note that formally deprecating them gives a basis for, for example, filtering these packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Crossing a message off does not make it safer or less safe, but it gives a clear reason to block it.
